chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Wartime schedule and unissued sides
summary: Edgar Sampson wrote on the road while the band worked nearly every night, with Army and Navy hospital shows and transcriptions.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: All right.
There were two other pieces -- two other selections. "Baby Don't Cry" and "Whatcha Say," which were never issued.
Did you have a hand in any of those in composing?
I think they were made the same time -- No, no.
Same date.
Same date. No, I didn't. I think Sampson made the arrangements, because Sampson -- I had Sampson doing a lot of things.
Edgar Sampson?
Yeah.
Because, you know, we were doing a lot of travelling all this time. Didn't have no time to write.
We were booked up every night a week. Only

nights we had off was maybe Sunday night. Would be one night. We had one night off a week, and we were booked, for like, three months solid.
One time, we were doing, like, the Coca-cola show every other week, and we were doing one nighters being transported around by the Army and Navy in planes, trucks and things, into the base.
We were doing benefits for the hospital and the -- you know, where they take the soldaërs before they ship them overseas?
Yeah.
We were going up in California, different spot where they had the soldiers. We weren't allowed to talk about where they were at -- you know, different place where they kept them.
But we would go in there and do a whole show with Velma Milton and the band. We do a whole hour and a half show for them.
And they would truck us right back out. And they had another --
Maybe in the afternoon or in the morning,
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
we do a Navy -- go to a Navy hospital and do a show. A Army hospital.
I know we did a Navy show in the morning at some hospital some place. And then we also do a Army show.
You did a number of transcriptions, apparently, with that band?
Yeah. Well, we did -- The transcriptions is something that -- I often wondered what they did with them. But I found out later what happened to them, you know.
Some of them are still around.
Yeah. We did a lot of transcriptions with Chick, too, also. We did a lot of transcriptions with Chick.
I was thinking of those United States Armed Services transcriptions.
Oh, yeah. That was -- the command performance was one of the best ones, I think -- one of the big ones.
I never heard that. I have the music to

it, but that was a dynamite thing. I would sure liked to hear that on tape, you know.
Yeah, I think (inaudible) --

We did a lot of transcriptions for overseas. Soldiers, we were talking to them, and things like that. And we'd go in the studios and do these transcription things, but I never heard them. Never knew what became of it. Like I say, it was during those times -- When you're travelling a lot as much as -- when you're travelling like two or three months out of a year, you know, every day, you're moving.
Sure, yeah.
Every day you're moving. You don't never know, you know --
Everything becomes a blur --
That's right.
-- what you do, (inaudible) recording.
They moving you so fast, you know.
